title: Ultrasound scans in pregnancy
intro: Ultrasound uses sound waves to create images of the baby in the womb. It is a safe, painless way to check the baby's growth and development and to date the pregnancy. Most women are offered several scans, and additional ones if there is a medical reason.

sections.heading: How it works
paragraphs: A probe is moved over your abdomen with gel, or in early pregnancy a smaller probe is placed in the vagina. It sends and receives sound waves that are converted into images. There is no radiation. Doctors use the lowest settings needed, and it is not used just for souvenir pictures without need.

sections.heading: Typical scans
paragraphs: The first scan, at around ten to twelve weeks, confirms the pregnancy, the number of babies, the heartbeat and the due date, and may include a measurement of the fluid behind the baby's neck as part of screening. A detailed scan at about twenty weeks examines the baby's organs, the placenta and the amount of fluid. A later scan checks growth and position.

sections.heading: What scans can and cannot show
paragraphs: Scans can detect many but not all structural differences, such as problems of the heart, spine or kidneys. Some conditions are not visible, and some findings are uncertain. A normal scan does not guarantee a healthy baby, and an abnormal finding does not always mean a serious problem. Image quality depends on the baby's position and on maternal factors.

sections.heading: If something unexpected is seen
paragraphs: If a scan shows a possible difference, you will usually be referred to a specialist for a more detailed scan and counselling. This can cause great worry. Ask for clear explanations, time to take in information and support. Options may include further tests, planning for treatment after birth, delivery in a specialist hospital or, depending on circumstances and law, other decisions.

sections.heading: Your choices
paragraphs: Scans are offered, and you can decide which to have. Think beforehand about what you would like to know, including whether you wish to learn the baby's sex. Bring a support person and write questions to ask. Extra scans without a medical reason are not recommended.

examples.title: Preparing for the detailed scan
examples.text: Imagine you have your twenty-week scan. You could ask beforehand what it can detect, who will explain the results and what happens if something is unclear.

examples.title: Handling uncertainty
examples.text: Suppose the scanner asks you to return for a repeat look. You might ask why, how common this is and how soon you will know more.

questions: Which scans will I be offered, and what are they for?
